# Introduction

Can political bulletins tell us something about party's level of centralization?

# Theory

The setup goes as follow. A national party $i$ seeks to gain as much
votes as possible in order to win an election. To achieve this, it has
to convince the local population across the whole country to i) turnout
on the day of the election, and ii) vote for party $i$. To do this, the
party dispose of resources which it can allocates across the different
constituencies to help promote certain candidates. The party $i$ also needs
to decide how *discretionary* its candidates can be in their campaign.
For simplicity, we will treat the allocation of resources as fixed for this
model, and focus exclusively on the *centralization* choice of party $i$.

The problem about centralization goes as follow. The leader of party $i$
does not know about the local needs and issues of all the constituencies.
Therefore, by imposing a low discretionary power to the candidates running
for its party, he runs the risk to alineate part of the electorate. His 
priorities might be situated far from those of the local population in 
constituency $d$.

# Data

This project collects an original data set using political bulletins in
Japan for the 2021, 2024, 2026 lower house elections.
